Supply-Trade and Commerce

subsubtopic: PREVENTION OF DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF COLOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Department of Trade and Commerce is, of course, one of the most important departments of government and covers a great range of activity, all of which is important to Canadians in all parts of this country. The minister is carrying a heavy burden, and I would like to congratulate him on the leadership and inspiration that he has given to all of those who have been associated with the marketing of Canadian grain in world markets.
During the past three years competition in the grain trade has multiplied, and it is a significant tribute to his efforts and those who carry out the details that sales of Canadian grain have been maintained at the high level at which they are today, which has characterized the record of this government since they came to office.
This year marks the 25th year of orderly marketing of western grain. Throughout that period of time great changes have taken place in both the production and the marketing of grain. Transportation patterns have changed somewhat, and in general there has been a gradual decline in the per capita consumption of flour. The Canadian wheat board was originally organized and created by a Conservative government, at the request of western farm organizations, to achieve the orderly movement and sale of wheat. That program was so overwhelmingly endorsed and supported by western grain producers that at a later date legislation was sought and achieved to bring oats and barley into the some operation.
On this occasion, when we are thinking in terms of the 25th anniversary of the formation of this board, I think it should be recorded here in the House of Commons that farmers are well satisfied with the operations of the board over that long period of years. It is true that there is some desire to see the effectiveness of the board improved and increased, but the substance of these suggestions is primarily a matter of government policy.
The value of orderly marketing has proven itself many times during the past 25 years, and the years of rust, frost and excessive moisture have vindicated the actions of the Conservative government which gave to the agricultural people of western Canada this instrument to protect themselves. Many of those who were strong opponents of orderly marketing 25 years ago have been converted, and about the only segment of the grain trade that remains aloof and alone to criticize orderly marketing are those who would like to see the futures market monopolize the marketing of Canadian grain.


There is one matter that I have discussed with the minister and members of the Canadian wheat board which has not been given the serious consideration that I would like to see. That is the situation with regard to those who have joined together to engage in a co-operative farm in order to try to improve their returns through the savings that can be made by pooling equipment, labour and resources. The arbitrary ruling now in effect concerning quotas discriminates against these people, and I am surprised that this matter has not been dealt with at this time, since it has been brought up many times. I would remind the minister that despite the fact that there are a limited number of people involved, it is a matter worthy of his usual brisk dispatch.
As hon. members all know, we have taken great pride in the standards set and maintained which have made Canadian wheat known throughout the world as hard red spring wheat. I wonder if the minister would give us some indication of the position with regard to the production of soft wheat in Canada, and the possibility of transferring some of our production along these lines to diversify our supply for prospective customers?
There is another matter that I have been asked about by many people, and it has to do with the progress being made by the small business section of the Department of Trade and Commerce. I assure the minister that there is a great deal of interest in this matter throughout the country, and the inquiries I get seem to indicate a desire for the extension of the services of this section. I wonder if the minister would give us a review of the present situation with regard to possible expansion of this branch.
Canada has been blessed with bountiful supplies of oil. Enterprising businessmen have dedicated their lives to the development of this resource. It is one of the most romantic chapters in the history of this country. There have been reports of oil imports from other countries into the natural marketing perimeter of some of our best oil reserves. I would like the minister to give us a summary of the position in regard to the import and export of petroleum products.
As hon. members are all aware, one of the great problems facing this country and its agricultural producers is the surplus of wheat which, while diminishing under the present administration, is still a matter of concern to all of us. I am heartily in agreement with the hon. member for Danforth and others who have indicated that more imagination could be brought to play in the marketing of all Canadian products. However, I am also convinced that part of the solution lies in

the encouragement of a balanced agriculture production. Several weeks ago I indicated that incentive prices under the stabilization program might be an effective aid in this regard. At this time I am thinking particularly of soybeans, and I should like to know if the minister could tell us whether there is any obstacle in the way, such as might affect our trade in general, to this government embarking upon a program to encourage soybean production in certain wheat producing areas in Canada with a view to reducing our total wheat production and supplying from Canadian farms the demand which apparently exists in this country for soybeans.
Finally, I should like to see placed on the record some indication of the situation with regard to wool and woollen products in so far as there products enter into our trade with other nations. I should be interested to know the value of imported woollen products, and I should also like to know if any raw wool has been imported. There are areas in western Canada where wheat is now being produced which are ideally suited for the production of wool and lambs. The past 10 or 12 years have seen the elimination of a number of textile plants along the St. Lawrence river, and I wonder whether the minister would care to venture an opinion as to the feasibility of promoting wool production and relocating of some of these plants in western Canada.
In conclusion I should like to compliment the minister on his realistic approach to Canada's trade problems. All of us admire the job he is doing. As we look out on the world today and realize the extent of the offensive now being mobilized against our way of life, an offensive that embraces and extends into all our trading problems, I cannot emphasize too strongly the importance of this country recognizing that offensive for what it is and taking the steps necessary to bring an awareness of the resulting problems and challenge to the attention of the general public. Those in industry at all levels must be brought face to face with the consequences of this offensive to everyone in our country unless some measure of sacrifice is made to maintain and expand our industrial capacity.
It would appear to me that some of the plants which have been closed down during the past 10 or 12 years were the victims of the rigidity of attitude of those who would not acknowledge that competition is the life blood of industrial well-being. The fault has not been with labour alone; it must be shared by management and owners as well. In a land so blessed with natural resources, inhabited by a people who pride themselves on their know-how, these closed factories and
Supply-Trade and Commerce manufacturing plants surely represent a challenge worthy of more initiative by those most directly concerned than has yet been apparent.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make some brief comments on a suggestion I have already made earlier in the present session. Government policies in Canada have been designed historically to support an underdeveloped country's economy, and especially its resources industries. Such past commercial policies that favoured resources industries and left the Canadian market open to all foreign competitors are responsible to a great extent for today's high level of unemployment. In fact, all plans for Canada's expanding prosperity have assumed that growth in manufacturing would provide jobs, income and higher living standards. This has not happened and is not happening.
Both as a provider of jobs and as a producer of goods Canadian manufacturing has been losing its earlier place in the Canadian 79951-0-498
Supply-Trade and Commerce economy. The 1955-57 boom in capital spending increased Canada's reliance on the construction industry as a provider of jobs, the very industry in which seasonal unemployment is the highest. Canada's cold climate, closing many outdoor industrial operations, always causes winter unemployment. There is always unemployment at any season when the business cycle turns downward. The business cycle has been turning upward since the autumn of 1958, but unemployment remains in some stubborn pockets. Hence a third category of built-in stationary unemployment has become apparent which does not readily yield to improving economic conditions or to the annual summer business spurt.
Technological factors, automation and the nation's monetary policies have been cited as reasons for these conditions. However, this chronic unemployment can become critical when the post-war baby boom makes its presence felt in the job market of the 1960's. Canada's population is now 17} million and will bounce up 27 per cent to 22J million by 1970, a 43 per cent increase in the job-seeking teen-age population alone. Unless the pace of industrialization quickens there will not be enough jobs to go around.
If manufacturing does not thrive, who will provide new jobs? This country has to develop enough industrial sinew to create an economy in which there is some healthy balance between manufacturing and resource development. We need domestic industries to supply the wants of the growing population and to provide employment for a large percentage of the labour force. We need to develop domestic industry in such a way as to reduce our propensity to import. Let me tell you, Mr. Chairman, that a new 100-man industry in any community will result in almost $1 million worth of new retail business in the community, in about 130 new homes, 65 new children, 185 more cars, 390 telephones and three new retail stores. Let me cite an editorial which appeared in the Montreal Gazette on August 8, 1960:
This is a good time to keep in mind the railway survey made of six Ontario and three Quebec cities, to determine the full impact of industrial development. This study, covering the years 1941 and 1951, showed that the addition of 100 new manufacturing workers meant to their community 427 more people; 131 more households; 66 more school children; 117 more workers employed other than in manufacturing; 187 more motor vehicle registrations; 393 more telephones; three more retail establishments, and nearly $1 million worth of increased retail sales per year.
When manufacturing can produce results like these for even 100 workers, it is obvious how important it is that everything possible should be done to encourage its growth in this country. Everybody benefits.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
It is especially the small industries, which are playing a very essential role in our economy, which have difficulties at the present time. They receive very limited financial help from the chartered banks and even from the industrial development bank. They need help, and their problems should be considered at the national level, on the same basis as those of the house builders, the western farmers, the maritime fishermen and others. Small industries have to be protected and multiplied even if only to ensure the stability of the country.
If you will permit me, Mr. Chairman, I should like to quote from a 1958 publication of the United States department of commerce:
During the past 10 years, two new types of credit organizations have evolved (in the United States) to help finance economic development-the development credit corporation and the development authority. Purpose of both is to provide long term risk capital to promising new and expanding industries that find themselves unable to meet the loan requirement of commercial banks and other financial institutions. Although both organizations derive from special legislation, the basic difference between them is that the credit corporation is a private organization depending entirely upon private sources to develop a loan fund. The authority, on the other hand, is an arm of the government with its loan fund originating, at least in part, from public sources.
This is what the article has to say about the credit corporation:
Legislation is required in forming a credit corporation to permit banks to accept institutional membership in the corporation. Such membership enables a bank to make available a small but specified percentage of its capital or surplus, or similar fund, to the corporation's credit pool. Thus, existing sources of capital can be tapped and the risk of a bad loan evenly distributed among institutional members and others.
In addition to institutional membership for financial organizations like banks, insurance, security and investment houses, stock is sold to private persons and other organizations. Management of the corporation affairs is handled through a board of directors, selected from stockholders, and by an executive committee usually elected by the institutional members.
On the other hand, the development authorities are getting their funds directly from public sources. What is urgently needed now in Canada is the creation of an organism to provoke industrial development, in the same way Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was created when the country was in dire need of housing. The first goal of this organism would be to make or guarantee loans for creating new industries or for maintaining and expanding existing ones. Its action would go far beyond the limited field of the present industrial development bank. Its operations would be based on a national program of development, taking into consideration the industrial capacity of
[Mr. Campeau.l
the country and its consumption requirements. Each individual loan would be considered in the light of this broad general program, according to a procedure similar to the one followed at the present time by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in the field of housing.
This proposed organism would encourage research and would thus bring extraordinary help to technical education. It would help us to keep within the country our outstanding scientists now deserting us for the United States. It would help to establish a sound immigration policy, the new immigrants to be absorbed by new industries. Finally, it would help in balancing efficiently our trade with foreign countries, by developing local industries capable of satisfying local needs and by diversifying our exported manufactured goods. By encouraging technical research, the new organism would encourage the creation of new products to be manufactured for local consumption and for export. Such a program would also permit Canada to compete efficiently against European trade blocs, especially the communist one, and also against the impact of the growing industrialization of underdeveloped countries.
Not only would the creation of this new organism be an efficient measure against increasing cyclical unemployment, but it would also become the basis of a well balanced national development program for the continued orderly growth of the whole country.

Mr. Chairman, I have been requested by certain organizations in British Columbia to have the minister comment with respect to a matter coming under this item. Until just over a year ago it was possible 79951-0-498i
Supply-Trade and Commerce to take out a blanket subscription for all the publications of the dominion bureau of statistics, and the fee was $60 a year. According to my information, if an organization still wanted all the publications it meant an increase in the fee from $60 to $420. I can understand the bureau wanting to obtain a return on the sale of their publications more commensurate with the cost, but an increase of approximately 600 per cent to 700 per cent in one fell swoop seems rather extraordinary.
I also happen to know that certain research bureaux in British Columbia proceeded, because of the change in policy, to subscribe for the publications they specifically wanted. I have in mind one bureau that subscribed for 43 publications in March of last year. In March of this year the bureau of statistics sent a subscription renewal notice at exactly the same fee as before, although during the year the organization did not receive all the publications for which it had subscribed. The organization paid the renewal fee although it had not received certain publications because they had not yet been published.
When they complained to the bureau of statistics they got what I consider a most peculiar answer. They were told that this happened on occasion because the publication was issued once every 14 months rather than once every 12 months, or perhaps was not issued even that frequently. The part I thought peculiar was that the bureau of statistics informed the research bureau in British Columbia that if they continued to pay their subscription fee for a period of five years it would work out that over that period of time they would receive all the publications for which they had subscribed. To me this appears to be a peculiar way to administer a business. It sounds more like a horse race or a lottery than a business administration, to be told that if you subscribe for five years you will receive all the publications at some time during that period.

This item for the dominion bureau of statistics is the one under which I assume we would discuss the work of the interdepartmental committee which has been asked to recommend a new official standard of measurement for unemployment. When we attempted to discuss this matter on the estimates of the Minister of Labour, Mr. Chairman, you will recall that he pointed out that it would be more appropriate to do so under the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I presume this is because the bureau of statistics is the agency of government which is most primarily concerned. At that time we on this side expressed the hope that when we came to this item, not only would we have a discussion of that matter but that the Minister of Labour might find it possible to be here to participate in that discussion.
This committee has been in existence for many months. It was set up, at least in part, as the result of a suggestion from this side of the house that the time had come when we should try to eliminate the confusion surrounding these statistics which are used to measure unemployment in this country. At the moment we have two separate sets of figures which have been used for some years, the bureau sample figures and the figures for registrations at the national employment

service offices. These figures never correspond. It has been suggested that the bureau figures are too low, and it has certainly been suggested that the national employment service figures are too high. In any event I think it is desirable, if it can be done, to resolve this problem by having one agreed standard of measurement which would be used in our discussions of this subject, thus avoiding some of the confusion that we have had in the past. Indeed, last Saturday the Prime Minister used as his figure for unemployment in a certain month in 1957 the national employment service registration figure which has been condemned by hon. members opposite on other occasions as being an exaggerated figure for unemployment in the country.
When the Minister of Labour announced the setting up of this interdepartmental committee on March 3 he said, and I quote from page 1702 of Hansard for that date:
Whenever a report Is forthcoming on this matter it will be made available to the house.
We on this side have been attempting to get that report before the house for some weeks so we would have it for consideration at this time when the estimates of trade and commerce are being examined. The minister has said for several weeks that the report was not ready, had not been completed, and that he was not solely responsible for it. It was an interdepartmental committee, and he was not able to do anything to hurry it up. He did say the other day however that the report had been completed and was before the cabinet for consideration. Last Saturday, as a matter of fact, the minister reported to the house that the government had received this report and he added, as reported on page 7679 of Hansard, that it would not be tabled until the government had reached a decision as to the recommendations contained therein.
This is a very different statement from the one he made on March 3, when he said that whenever the report was forthcoming it would be made available to the house. Now we are told that it will not be made available to the house until the government reaches a decision in regard to it. It seems to me these two statements are not consistent.
I repeat what I have just said. We still think it is important that we should agree, if we can, in this house on the most appropriate standard of measurement for unemployment. If agreement can be reached, we should use that figure so that at least this complex technical question will not become a partisan issue. So far as we are concerned, we are prepared to take a responsible attitude toward this matter, providing we are not
Supply-Trade and Commerce subjected to a fait accompli by the government and provided we are not told that the decision has been made, that a certain measure for unemployment is being accepted while there has been no opportunity of considering the matter in any way in the House of Commons prior to that decision being taken. We think, therefore, there should be no unilateral action taken in this matter, even if this may mean a slight delay, until there has been an opportunity to discuss it and get agreement if possible in the house.
For that purpose, Mr. Chairman, I have two suggestions to make. The first is that the report of the joint committee which is now before the government should be made available to the house immediately, as the Minister of Labour indicated on March 3 would be done, so that we can see it today and study it.
My second request is that no action be taken with regard to any recommendations in this report before the next session, because it is quite obvious that there will be no time now for the kind of examination which it deserves and which its importance warrants. We suggest that at the very beginning of the next session this report should be referred to the standing committee on industrial relations so that its authors and other experts could be examined by members of that committee and the report made clear by those who drafted it to members who are concerned that there should be from such a report, a single measurement of unemployment which would be acceptable to all members of the house.
It seems to me that only if that procedure is followed can we be sure that the new measurement, if there is to be a new measurement, will meet the approval of the house itself; and if it does not meet the approval of the house generally then there is not much likelihood that we are going to avoid in the future a difference of opinion over measurements such as we have had in the past.
It is for that reason, Mr. Chairman, that I bring this matter up, and it is for that reason that I have made these two suggestions.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are grateful, I am sure, to the Leader of the Opposition for bringing up this matter. It is a matter which I have brought forward on orders of the day not less than seven times during the course of the present session. This could easily be one of the most important matters that we will be discussing at this tail end of the session.
Unemployment is undoubtedly the most important domestic problem in Canada. It has persisted now since 1957 in serious proportions. Unemployment at the present time on the basis of the latest available figures issued by the minister's department, through the bureau of statistics, reveals that we have unemployment at a higher level at this time than at any period since 1935.
When this question was vigorously pursued during the course of the session the Minister of Labour, I believe largely to remove himself from any embarrassment, sought to indicate that the government was going to ask for a consideration of a new standard of measurement of unemployment in Canada.
It is important to keep in mind what are the present standards of measurement. They are the standards employed by the dominion bureau of statistics, based on a sampling of some 30,000 or so individuals in our country. There is also the figure provided by the national employment service, which I believe to be a more accurate figure because it is actually founded on the end of the day reports in our unemployment offices in Canada. The dominion bureau of statistics figure is nothing more than what it purports to be, a sampling of unemployment in our country. A sampling cannot take into account heavy concentrations of unemployment. Then, there is what I believe to be the irresistible figure, made up of the number of people actually in receipt of unemployment insurance benefits.


Because there are these three sets of figures the government has suggested that it is confused and that the public mind is confused as well. I believe there is no confusion. Each of these three sets of figures indicates nothing more than what each purports to establish. However, the fact is that the government, having established this mirage of confusion, did decide to set up an interdepartmental committee. That was over four and a half months ago. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says he is not charged with this matter, that this is a matter which comes under the responsibility primarily of the Minister of Labour. The Minister of Labour contended, when we were discussing his estimates, and he was pressed strongly, that this was a matter which came within the authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I do not know which minister is primarily responsible, but the bureau of statistics is a division in my hon. friend's department. I believe that if he could definitely assure the committee, as he has so co-operatively indicated today, that this matter would be open for discussion in parliament when we next meet before this question is finalized, there would be no difficulty today. But I believe we have to have that definite assurance.
The situation is not as easy as the minister's co-operative attitude this morning suggested. The industrial relations committee met this winter. It had one meeting. That was an organization meeting, for the purpose of electing a distinguished member of this house as its chairman. There is before that committee a motion in the name of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, to the effect that the committee should give study to the various standards of measurement of unemployment in Canada.
The chairman of that committee asked the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, if he would not proceed with the motion at that particular time, so it could be considered at a subsequent meeting which, we were told, would be called shortly. That meeting has never been called. We have asked in this house that a meeting of the industrial relations committee take place so that motion could be disposed of. We have not been able to receive from the government or from the chairman of the committee any co-operation whatsoever, with the result that for five and a half months this motion of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has stood in suspense.
Now, the Minister of Labour told me a week ago-ten days ago or thereabouts, to be precise-that he did not know whether

the interdepartmental committee had made its study. When pressed that he should himself initiate an inquiry as to whether the study had been completed, he very reluctantly agreed. Then three or four days ago he announced that the study had been completed and that a report was in the hands of the government. When asked by the Leader of the Opposition, when that report would be made available for consideration in this house, he said that the cabinet had not yet had an opportunity to consider it.
I want, first of all, to submit that I doubt very much if this is a matter for the cabinet at all. This is a matter of procedure to be determined by the bureau of statistics in co-operation with other departments, and it seems to me somewhat unusual, that the government of Canada should want to interfere in a technical matter of this kind. It is a technical matter, because the assessment made by the bureau of statistics must be in accordance with standards about which the government as such cannot be expected to have any expert knowledge. In any event, we have not yet on this, possibly the second last day of this session, or even the last-

-we have not had from the Minister of Labour, who has been wholly uncommunicative with regard to all these questions that concern unemployment, any information whatever as to whether or not the government considering this report or whether parliament will have an opportunity of examining the recommendations.
I feel that this is an extremely important matter. We can only determine the degree of unemployment in our country in accordance with the standards of measurement that are used. We are shortly to prorogue. We shall in all probability not come back here until next January, 1961. Every indication seems to suggest that unemployment will be as severe this fall and next winter as it has been in the previous periods. We do not want, in the interval between prorogation and the opening of a new session of parliament, unemployment to assume serious proportions while we, as members of parliament, are placed in a position where, because of the adoption of new standards, we are not able to determine that fact.
If the minister will give us an assurance today-and it must be today, I believe- before we can pass this item that parliament will not be denied the opportunity of examining this particular report before any change is made, then the minister will, I am sure, have the knowledge that the passage of his estimates is going to proceed
Supply-Trade and Commerce without any trouble. The hon. gentleman has been co-operative today-much more cooperative than the Minister of Labour-and if he can give us this assurance that there is not going to be any change made in this standard of measurement without parliament being given the opportunity to know whether any proposed change is a sound one or a desirable one-

speechtext: The hon. member has just said it was not necessary for the government to consider this report.

speechtext:
I said exactly that, but if the government is going to concern itself with it, it must also be a matter for parliament. I feel keenly about this, speaking as I do for an industrial part of Canada, where there is heavy unemployment.
Before resuming my seat I want to say that we have contended all along, as did the hon. gentleman, that the national employment service figure is the most reliable of all, and we had confirmation of that view in the well-balanced, controlled speech made by the Prime Minister last Saturday afternoon, when he himself referred to unemployment in 1955, using the national employment service figure, thereby confirming the contention which the Leader of the Opposition and other members of this parliament have been makng during the course of this session.

The minister has suggested that a little time might be given him to consider this matter. Our request is surely a reasonable one. The minister must have known it would be brought up; we made it clear to the Minister of Labour that we were going to bring it up on these estimates, because this would be the only occassion when we could discuss it. As my hon. friend has said, we would like an assurance that action will not be taken on this matter without parliament having a chance to consider it. Otherwise we may find ourselves in the next session confronted with an entirely new measurement at a time when the standard of measurement will be very important, without ever having been given an opportunity to discuss that new standard so it could be an agreed one. That is what we are asking the minister, and I think it is a reasonable request.
The hon. gentleman is asking for a little time to consider, and I think that is a reasonable reaction. Perhaps we could allow this item to stand, and while consideration is being given to this question we can go on with the rest of the estimates. I am sure the hon. member for Essex East was not attempting to threaten in any way, shape or form.

In the Canadian wheat
board report there is a table given at page 15. It deals with the crop years and covers the period from the 1945-46 crop year up to 1958-59. My concern is that the figures for 1958-59 show Canada as having 23.9 per cent of the total world export trade in wheat. The minister used a figure for the year 1958 of some 35.7 per cent. I took it to be the minister's argument that we had increased our share of the world market. My understanding of the situation is that we are in some difficulties and have a relatively smaller part of the world market than we had in earlier years, certainly not a better one. That is the point I want cleared up.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: PREVENTION OF DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF COLOUR

The hon. member for Ottawa West is correct in what he is saying. Here we are getting into two statistical tables which we had better straighten out right

away. I was giving the figures for the commercial situation. I gave the figure of 35.7 per cent in 1958 as Canada's share of world trade in commercial markets. When you take Canada's share in the total world trade of wheat including the concessional items, the gift programs of our country, the United States and others, Canada's share is 24.2 per cent. That is a decline of 6 per cent from the years 1920 to 1939. The United States percentage increased quite substantially from the period 1920-39 to 1958 due to a great increase under PL480 gifts of wheat to underdeveloped countries.
The hon. member said something about some danger here. It is not a loss of Canada's markets that has been suffered at all. In fact, as I pointed out, we have in the last three years maintained our position as the leading commercial wheat salesmen in the world. We have maintained our position with regard to our share of the wheat that is sold for actual cash. The activities of the United States under PL480 has not seriously affected Canada's sales abroad, as I have shown. Through co-operation with the United States authorities we are taking the necessary steps to see that as markets develop for wheat in other countries, in Asia and Africa, we will have an opportunity to participate in those markets when they become commercial markets.
That is one of the reasons we are sitting in with the United States in discussions of wheat disposal programs. That is one reason Canada is participating in these programs, and that is one reason we are actively engaged in making certain that if new markets develop in Asia or Africa, Canadian wheat or flour will be considered. At the moment I do not see any particular danger to Canada in the fact that her share of the total exports of wheat is somewhat less than it was 20 years ago, because she has maintained her position in the commercial markets of the world.

subsubtopic: PREVENTION OF DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF COLOUR

I thank the minister for clarifying the matter of the statistics he was using. That clarification is wholly satisfactory as far as I am concerned and explains what the difficulty was. The conclusions the minister draws from the statistics are somewhat different from mine, but the statistical fact is that our percentage of he market on any basis is down from the period between the wars, and our percentage of the total export of wheat, taking more recent periods, is down too.
I realize the difficulty of picking out particular statistics, but it is interesting to take the three crop years 1951-52, 1952-53 and 1953-54. Our share varied from 32 per cent
Supply-Trade and Commerce to 39 per cent of the total wheat exports of the world in those years and are now down to 23.9 per cent in 1958-59. I am prepared to admit that that was unusually high in the years 1951-54. Then we came into an era of programs sometimes called give-away programs, under which wheat is given by some countries to others on a basis of other than commercial sales, and our percentage share of the total exports dropped sharply. It seems to me that indicates a matter for real concern today, and this is a situation that has to be watched closely.
The fact is that viewed by any criteria we are down in our wheat exports. Our reduction in percentage of total world trade coincides in timing with the expansion in the type of program under which gifts are made to other countries. The problem is also complicated by the uncertainty of'the access of our agricultural products to the United Kingdom and European markets because of the relationship of the United Kingdom with the trade areas of Europe. As far as I am concerned it is the cause of some alarm.
I am one of those who recognize that the marketing of our wheat is of the utmost importance. I think I may be permitted to make this comment. In the wide-ranging debate that took place yesterday it seemed to me there tended to be not sufficient recognition of the problems of the marketing of wheat and the huge carryovers in this country. It is of the utmost concern to the whole economy of the country. It is not just a problem of the western wheat farmers; its impact falls on them primarily but it is a problem of the whole economy of the country, and for that reason I make no apology for raising this question for the consideration of the committee or for drawing it to the attention of the minister.
There are other aspects that could be developed, of course. There is the whole matter of the development of exports to Japan. I hope great foresight will be used in developing and exploiting that market to our best advantage. I recognize that it will require some steadiness and some resourcefulness, and also some resistance to pressures which may arise in connection with our trade with that country, but I hope it is something that the minister will bear very much in mind.

May I say one final word with regard to wheat. I appreciate the hon. member's remarks, and he is quite right in saying that this is not the sole concern of the western farmers. It is primarily their livelihood, but it is of concern to all Canada

Supply-Trade and Commerce because of the surpluses we have been carrying and the importance of wheat in our general export trade. We should not minimize the importance of that whatsoever, but our surplus situation 'has been materially improved in the last three years. In July, 1957 it was estimated that in this country we had a surplus of 730 million bushels, and this was before the new crop of 1957 was harvested. That surplus situation has been reduced in the course of the last three years by certainly over 200 million bushels. I think now the surplus stands at something over 500 million bushels.

subsubtopic: PREVENTION OF DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF COLOUR
speechtext: It is 566 million bushels.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: PREVENTION OF DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF COLOUR
speechtext: That is quite a sharp reduction from the surplus of 730 million bushels three years ago. I am not sure whether the hon. member for Ottawa West mentioned anything about the decline in our wheat exports. Percentagewise, with regard to world trade, he may be able to show that but in actual fact, over the last three years-

speechtext: -there has been an increase in our export position. I gave the figures at page 7713 of Hansard, showing that in the 1957-58 crop year we exported 320.3 million bushels; in 1958-59 we exported 249.1 million bushels, and estimates for the crop year that has just closed are 276.7 million bushels, making an average of roughly 297 million bushels for each of those three years, which is above the average for the preceding three years when it was 276 million bushels. The preceding 10-year average was 284.4 million bushels and the 30-year average was 252.6 million bushels. Therefore we are really doing better in our export business now than we were before.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I can say just a word about this because of the importance of the matter. I understand that in the first 10 months of this year the world trade in wheat was up about 6 per cent and our percentage was down about 3 per cent. The minister has explained the reason for that. It was due largely, though not entirely, to non-commercial sales by the United States; but of course we have also increased our sales by special arrangements, although not quite to the same extent as has the United States. If we are going to make comparisons of cash sales we have to take Canadian cash sales against United States cash sales.
The minister has pointed out that there has been close co-operation and liaison maintained with the United States in respect of those non-commercial sales in order to ensure that when they become commercial


sales, if they ever do, we shall have an opportunity to participate in the increased commercial marketing which will result. Of course that is very important if it can be brought about. It can only be brought about by our own effort and by the co-operation the minister has spoken about with the United States, and I do not suppose this situation is likely to change very much in the next year or two; certainly not to our advantage, because while our own surplus has gone down, as the minister has pointed out, from about 734 million bushels to 566 million bushels, I think I am correct in saying that the United States surplus has gone up. Therefore there will be the same, if not greater, pressure on them to force that surplus in some way or other on to the world's markets. We are going to be up against this problem for some time.
Then we also have another factor, namely the competition we are encountering from the Soviet union, not very serious at the present time except perhaps in the Netherlands, where I understand there has been some Soviet grain marketing to our disadvantage. In any event, it is not only an important matter; it is a matter which causes anyone concerned with it some anxiety.
I will just put on the record the figures for July 22, as published by the dominion bureau of statistics, which show exactly what the situation is in terms of the number of bushels shipped during the August-May period of this year, which is the period I am talking about. I am quoting from the bulletin which says:
Total exports of wheat and wheat flour in terms of wheat from these four countries-
The four main exporters.
-in the first 10 months (August-May) of the current Canadian crop year totalled 821 million bushels, some 6 per cent above the 771.5 million bushels exported during the same months of 1958-59.
Then it goes on to say this, and this is the reason for our worries:
Shipments from each of the four countries during the August-May period this year were as follows, with the preceding year's corresponding totals in brackets (in millions): United States, 425.4 bushels (380.6); Canada, 235.9 ( 243.8); Argentina, 62.8 (85.5); and Australia, 96.9 (61.6).
These figures show that the United States during this period has shipped, if my calculation is correct, 109 million bushels more wheat on the world market than we have. The minister has said-and I am not challenging his figures because I do not know; I accept them-that we are still maintaining our superiority in cash shipments over United States exports. If that is the case, that would mean that during those 10 months the United States has thrown on the world market in a non-commercial way 190 million bushels of wheat, which is a very dramatic measure of

That is quite correct. There has been a great movement of United States wheat into world markets but not into commercial markets. Seventy per cent of United States exports of wheat are going forward under their gift program to the countries that need it. The figures for 1958 indicate that Canada exported to commercial markets -I take this from the United States publication to which I was referring-270 million bushels compared with exports by the United States of 142 million bushels. That was in 1958, and it shows the difference in commercial sales between the two countries.
However, we are also participating in the export of wheat by way of an assistance program similar to that of the United States in some respects. Under the Colombo plan we have shipped a substantial amount of wheat out of this country over the last eight years. I have a table here which might be of interest to hon. members and perhaps could be incorporated in Hansard. It is not in any partisan spirit that I refer to the fact that shipments have been higher in the last few years than in the earlier years. Rather it is an indication that the whole program of gifts to underdeveloped countries has been expanding. If hon. members would like to have this table printed in Hansard it will give a picture of the gift program and the loan program that have been in effect now for a number of years. For the last three years the figures have been running this way. We have given by outright gift some 36,362,697 bushels of wheat or wheat in the form of wheat flour, valued at $60,649,968. On a loan basis we have shipped from Canada 21,560,795 bushels of wheat valued at $34,999,999.
Therefore in the last three years the wheat and flour export program under the Colombo plan by way of outright gift or by way of long term loan has amounted in total to approximately 58 million bushels valued at approximately $95J million. We are sharing in the program to assist countries that require food, and we are doing it by outright gift and by long term loans.

subsubtopic: PREVENTION OF DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF COLOUR
speechtext:
I think the minister's figures as to our share of non-commercial marketing in the world are quite interesting, and I am not complaining about the growth of these figures. It is quite true that in the last three years, as the minister has pointed out, our wheat marketings under the Colombo plan have become substantially greater than they were in previous years when we were operating under the Colombo plan. However, I am also quite sure that in those earlier
years under the Colombo plan there was a great reluctance on the part of recipient countries to include consumer goods such as wheat, wheat flour and things like that within the programs of assistance which we were negotiating with them. As the minister knows, the Colombo plan is a plan for technical and capital assistance, and there was quite considerable reluctance to have that pattern of assistance altered in those earlier years. The fact that these increases have been made in recent years is an indication not only that we have a lot of wheat to dispose of but that the recipient countries have altered to some extent at least their attitude toward assistance under Colombo plan arrangements of that kind.

speechtext: That is quite true, and I am glad the Leader of the Opposition has added that point. Parliament approved an increase in Colombo plan aid from $35 million to $50 million, and of that increase the larger amount has gone into the provision of surplus food for countries that need it. The Leader of the Opposition is quite right that prior to that the Colombo plan funds were primarily intended for capital investment and improvement in those countries. Nevertheless, even under those circumstances and with the reluctance of the receiving countries to take food rather than capital assistance, there was a substantial program in the preceding five years from 1952 to 1957. Outright gifts amounting to 10,814,436 bushels were made in the five years I have mentioned, having a value of $29,142,059.

I should like to ask the minister a question or two on the oil situation, based on the progress that has been made

in achieving the objective for domestic marketings set out in the report of the Borden commission. I have made some calculations based on some figures which I was able to secure and which I should like put on the record. Perhaps the minister will comment on them. I hope they are accurate, but if they are not I am sure he will correct them.
These figures cover the first six months of the current year and deal with the consumption of crude oil, first. They show, too, that domestic consumption during this period of six months in 1960 totalled 78,675,000 barrels against 75 million barrels for the same period in 1959. In other words the consumption of domestic crude has gone up, but the consumption of imported crude also has gone up to 57 million barrels from around 55 million barrels.
Now, if I may call them that, the Borden report totals-we are within five months of the date on which these totals were to be reached-were 700,000' barrels of Canadian oil per day. That would amount to a figure for the six-month period of about 128 million barrels. We are therefore a long way from reaching this Borden total with only five months to go. The progress has not been as rapid as some hoped it would be. I have seen it stated by some experts that in the light of the experience of the first year, it may take about three years to reach that objective of 700,000 barrels a day. This means that very soon the government will be faced with the problem of deciding what to do about this matter. We are about five months from the date fixed by the Borden commission, but we are a long way from the objective. The increase in the consumption of Canadian crude in Ontario has been very modest indeed.
I ask the minister, therefore, if he can tell us what the plans of the government are for dealing with this matter. We had a statement a few weeks ago in which he said this would be a major problem for the government, and it would be given immediate consideration. Perhaps I could put on the record a paragraph from a column dealing with this matter which appeared in the Vancouver Sun, written by Mr. Gerald Waring, dated July 22, 1960. At the very end of his column he had this to say:
And if it proved that -western oil could be competitive with imported oil, it would put the west-east pipe line proposal on a sounder base.
This speculation, of course, leaps far ahead of the existing situation. The government apparently has not made up its mind yet about requiring the Montreal refineries to accept western oil on a quota basis, and will not until parliament is out of the way-[DOT]
I hope parliament is almost out of the way. Perhaps I should not put it in that form, but parliament is likely to be out of the way before long.

But this is the direction in which the government will have to move, if it decides to catch the ball batted by the Borden commission.
In other words, the government will have to move in the direction of doing something to meet the objective set down in the commission report which apparently, and the minister will correct me if he thinks I am wrong, is not being met by other marketing forces.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition has raised a problem of considerable magnitude. It is a problem which is very complex in its ramifications. The Borden commission produced two excellent reports, one on gas and one on oil. The second one, on oil, has been very carefully studied by the national energy board and by the government, and we are fortunate in having set up the national energy board where people can devote their whole time to problems of such importance to Canada as gas and oil.
The national energy board, as hon. members are aware, will have been in operation for just one year on October 1, and in the course of that time has wrestled with the extremely difficult problem of the export of gas and the number of applications which have come before it, and it has settled some of those problems. It has facing it the consideration of a number of applications concerning the export of electricity by Canada which has been conducted on a year to year basis, and before renewal of those applications public hearings have to be held and the consideration of the national energy board must be given to them.
Superimposed upon those two great problems has been that of oil. Canada is blessed with great quantities of oil. It has a great developing oil industry which feels that it could move much more rapidly if certain decisions were made or if the export market were enlarged, and naturally we are concerned, as is every Canadian, with the development of national resources and the importance of gas and oil.
The oil industry has become substantial and well established in western Canada; its problems are known to the government and to the Canadian people, and were reviewed in the report of the Borden commission. In the course of that report certain targets were set as being acceptable in order to sustain and enlarge the oil industry so that the productive capacity of that industry in Canada, certainly in western Canada, could be increased; because following upon that would come exploration to discover more oil and one thing leads to another. This enlarges the opportunity for other employment, and

Supply-Trade and Commerce makes available to Canadians a source of power which is essential in modern times, and as exploration continues maps out the reserves on which we can base plans for the future development of Canada.
The Borden commission report indicated that if a production target could be reached of 700,000 barrels per day, that would be a great help to the industry, and it indicated that a period of time should be permitted to allow the industry a chance to adjust itself to that production. It examined the consumption requirements in Canada and the export possibilities in the United States, and over the last year along with the energy board I have been watching closely the developments in the oil industry and the situation with regard to our export markets in the United States. We see the problem more clearly and appreciate the difficulties which face us.
The obvious market for the export of Canadian oil is of course the United States, but there are some difficulties there with competition from other sources. There are obvious large markets in Canada, but whether they should be sustained by oil from other sources or from Canadian sources is a matter yet to be determined because there are so many factors involved. Again, it cannot be a matter for easy generalization; there are too many complicated factors for a quick or early decision which would not be based upon sound information.
The situation at the moment is this, and I stated this in the house some time ago. It is a matter of priority for the government, and the responsibility rests with us to determine some of the aspects with regard to the oil industry and try to forecast the future. At the present stage of progression I have asked the energy board to assemble the information which is required so that a proper decision can be made. That involves bringing up to date the statistical information contained in the Borden report and adding fresh information that is perhaps now in the hands of the energy board or can be obtained from the industry itself; then setting up the various problems which face the oil industry not only with regard to our domestic market but with regard to our export market.
In order to make a proper assessment of that we have to know the situation in the United States with regard to their policy on imports of oil, and we have to know something about the world situation with regard to the production of oil. It has become one of the great problems facing us at this time, and before too long I hope we will have available all the facts and figures which are required to reach a decision in order that a proper, and sound policy for the whole industry in Canada can be formulated.

I do not foresee any easy route in reaching the decisions which are required. The problem is not without great complications, and we have to consider, as we did with the subject of gas, the question of reserves and Canadian requirements and try to forecast the future. Fortunately the Borden commission made a very extensive study of the oil industry, and that will be the foundation on which we will move forward in the course of the next few months to determine what should be done. We expect the interest of the provinces and the co-operation of industry in this search for a solution, and I am sure that in the field of power, whether it is electricity, gas, oil or atomic energy, Canada as a whole is very much interested; because it is on the basis of power, and cheap power from whatever source, that the industrial strength of Canada can be maintained.
These factors and others are now being considered. I cannot say when the studies will be completed, but they are already under way. The national energy board is now fortunately organized and experienced, and will be of great help to the government in assembling this information and presenting advice based on the knowledge and experience which is essential with regard to an industry that has such great complexity as the oil and gas industry of Canada.
That is as far as I can go in answer to the question of the Leader of the Opposition. We are apprised of the problem; we are working on it, and we hope before long to present to parliament and the public our views with regard to the oil industry of Canada. This is a matter which will be awaited with a great deal of interest and even with impatience in some quarters, but we feel it is better to move slowly and effectively rather than to rush in without all the facts being at our disposal.
I think all members will agree that the action taken in this regard should be based on a study of all the facts available in order to reach a sound conclusion. The decision with regard to gas exports has given a great stimulus to the whole of the petroleum industry which, of course, is as much interested in gas as in oil. With that background of experience and sound decision I think we can rely on the energy board to bring forward sound proposals with regard to this other problem that confronts us. As I indicated some time ago, this is a priority task, and it is being treated in that manner.

I think the committee will be grateful to the minister for the statement he has been able to make on a subject of such great importance to our national development as the development of a national oil

policy. As the minister has said, and as I am sure we all agree, there is no easy route to the solution of the problems he has mentioned, and I am sure the minister is grateful that the national energy board is at his disposal to give him advice on this and other matters. Perhaps I might be permitted to pay my tribute to the manner in which that board is working.
It is true that the Borden commission made an expert and exhaustive survey of this question, and as a result of that survey the commission came to the conclusion that the Canadian oil industry could live-and I am paraphrasing what was said-reasonably comfortably with a situation which would permit them to market 700,000 barrels a day. Five months from the date which was set for this result that figure has not, of course, been realized, and I suspect it will not be realized in any event unless there can be increased access to the United States market. The minister has said that is the obvious market for a large proportion of our production, and of course that is true. But there is nothing, to a layman at least, very obvious about the way in which the oil industry works in the United States. While it is true that in a well-ordered continental society, if we really had continental co-operation and consolidation in these matters, that is where a great proportion of our oil production should be going, there are forces, as the minister knows better than I do, which are working against such a development; forces not only of domestic competition which will reflect themselves in domestic political action, but forces which arise no doubt because an industry which may be domestic is also very international in its scope. Therefore the great corporations have to weigh their interests in Canadian supplies against their interests in those from Saudi Arabia, Venezuela as well as from the United States itself. So the development of a national oil policy which will ensure the exploitation of these great oil resources for the benefit of Canada will have, shortly, to be undertaken.
We can talk about this subject at length, though I am not sure whether anybody wishes to do so at this time, but I should like to ask the minister if he is reasonably satisfied as to the situation with regard to United States action that may be taken to interfere with the increase in our marketing in that country. I know that within the last year or so ago this stupid argument that the United States government should take action against our imports on grounds of security has been dropped. There could be nothing much more unreal than that kind of argument, but there are other considerations at
Supply-Trade and Commerce work, and perhaps the minister might be in a position to give his own views as to whether we are likely to be faced with less or greater restrictions as we try to reach this market, which is the natural market for such a high proportion of our oil production.

As a member of the special committee on research I should like to make a few comments at this time, but in view

Supply-Trade and Commerce of the hopes and aspirations that we hear voiced around the corridors today I shall try to make them very brief.
In the six or eight meetings of this special committee on research which we were able to hold it was necessary to confine ourselves to the general policy of organization and administration. The offices of the national research council prepared especially for this research committee the little pamphlet I hold in my hand, which I suppose I could refer to as the little grey book. In my view it is a very fine summary of the work of the council. I hope the minister or the president of the national research council will see to it that this publication receives wider circulation than just hon. members of the House of Commons or members of the special committee on research. This booklet certainly gives a fine idea of the work done by the council. Because of that fact and because it is written in layman's language I think it should be widely distributed throughout the country. My reason for saying that is that it gives an excellent idea of the work being done by the council, not only in Canada, but also the successful efforts that are being made by the council to rank Canadian science with that of other countries of the world.
As I said before, there was time to discuss only in a limited way the organization of the council. I suggest to the minister that there are many more interesting phases of the work of this council which could be gone into. I suggest to him that this committee be resumed early in the next session so that many of the interesting things that can be considered in the committee may be discussed with the officers of the national research council.
I suppose it is true that some of the work that council is doing has resulted from tasks which it was given some years ago and which perhaps do not now form a very important part of its work. I refer particularly to the Canadian government specifications board. The work of this board probably could be more properly delegated to some branch of the treasury board. Perhaps the minister will see fit to recommend transferring it from the national research council to some other appropriate authority.
Those who came before the committee at its meetings were able to assure us of the fine work which is being done and tell us of the contribution that is being made by Canadian scientists to world science in general. I should like to commend the work of Dr. Steacie and his associates, who were most anxious to give to members of the committee all the information they thought was pertinent to the various topics discussed. They went to all sorts of

trouble to provide facts and figures which were not contained in the grey book, and were very anxious to give satisfaction to all hon. members of the committee. For that I wish to thank Dr. Steacie and those associated with him.
The council established in 1916, then known as the national advisory council for scientific and industrial research and now known as the national research council, was at that time a very small body. Even in 1917 it consisted of only 11 men. Those 11 men began a survey of Canada's scientific resources. Two things followed from that survey. First, it became very evident that industrial research was almost non-existent in Canada. Second, it was recognized that the national supply of research personnel was most inadequate. In our universities at that time we found university personnel almost completely absorbed in undergraduate work. There was little time for research. Graduate scholarships were lacking, and most of our postgraduate students took their training outside the confines of Canada. Only a small percentage of them returned to this country.
The council was able to set up a system of scholarships and grants so successful that today they form an important part of its present activities. The council has been able not only to do its own work but has given a great impetus to research in industry which has been improved over the years. It is now rapidly approaching the point where industrial research in Canada is becoming equal to industrial research in other countries.
Here in Canada, of course, we have a number of problems that require research. I am sure that in industry and in defence there is a great need for research on ore. We know there is a great need for medical research, too. Most of that type of research is now being done by the universities and is sponsored by the national research council. A great deal more could be done along that line than is now being done.
We should also have research done on the transmission of electrical power. I speak of that because it is of particular importance to my province, where we have a large potential on the Hamilton river, something exceeding 5 million horsepower. If it were possible to devise some method of transmitting this power the value of that source of energy would be much more important than it is today. We have stretching across this continent, and particularly in the west, pipe lines transmitting oil and gas, other forms of energy. There is no reason why we should not have a grid across this country transmitting electrical power, particularly when we have the sources that will supply that power.

As hon. members know, electrical power is transmitted by alternating current at high voltage for relatively short distances. If electricity has to be transmitted at high voltage for distances beyond 700 or 800 miles some difficulty arises. In some countries in Europe a great deal of research has been done with respect to the transmission of electricity over long distances by transmitting the electricity in direct current form rather than in alternating current form. I hope the national research council will gather some information regarding the possibility of transmitting electrical energy in Canada over long distances at high voltage by means of direct current.
I was referring to the growth of the national research council. Twenty years ago only 300 people were employed by the council. Today we have 722 employees on the scientific staff, 972 on the technical staff and 896 on the administrative and service staff, making a total of approximately 2,600 employees, and this even without the defence research and atomic energy employees.
The efforts of the council have provided not only much of the scientific research required in Canada, but have made a contribution to scientific knowledge in general. Reference was made in the committee hearings to the scientific journals and I shall comment further on those. At page 121 of the fourth volume of the minutes and proceedings of the special committee on research Dr. F. T. Rosser explained that the journals of the national research council enjoyed a wide circulation. He said:
The journals go into every country in the world that has important scientific institutions. I have given you the figures for Russia, and the Chinese figures are even larger than Russia's. There are 315 subscriptions going into 14 institutions in China; and, on exchange, there are 19 subscriptions in 5 institutions. This is true all around the world. The same is happening in every country that is progressing scientifically.
Dr. Steacie went on to say:
Thirty or forty years ago there were just the odd small groups which were internationally well known. There has been a very big increase since. The net result is that scientifically, rather than being in the backwoods we have now become one of the important scientific countries of the world.
I think we have reached this status largely because of the efforts of the national research council. Its journals, of course, are the publications of the work done by the council and are the end product and the permanent record of the research work carried on. We know that our research work here in Canada is very acceptable to many other countries of the world, and perhaps two reasons can be cited for that assumption. First, the journals find their way into the scientific libraries of all the major countries of the world; second, Canadian scientists now publish their papers
Supply-Trade and Commerce in the Canadian journals, where years ago the papers were published in the journals of foreign countries.
In 1945-47 the average total pages for the Canadian journals was 1,710; the average for 1957-59 was 7,722. Circulation in May, 1960 totalled over 10,000, with 4,000 in Canada and over 6,000 in foreign countries. I recite these figures just to show the progress which has been made by the national research council and the effort which is being made to distribute scientific knowledge gained in Canada to the rest of the world.
The basic functions of the national research council, as I understand them, are the promotion of scientific research, the operation of laboratories, and university research in Canada; and in these three functions, I believe Canada is being well served. The council should be given every opportunity to expand its activities in its own way either in fundamental or applied research.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I again suggest to the minister that this committee be continued next year, so that perhaps many of the most interesting problems relating to the national research council can be discussed at that time.
