Mr. Chairman, as we take up this item, I draw to the attention of the committee and of the authorities a matter which, for more than three years, has provoked much comment and annoyance among people in northwestern Quebec. I refer to the experiments being made in that area of the province for the purpose of inducing artificial rainfall by seeding clouds with crystals of silver iodide vaporized in generators commonly referred to as "rainmaking machines", or by means of aircraft.
To introduce the subject, I had better quote some excerpts of an article published in the L'Echo Abitibien of July 21, 1960, under the heading:
June rainfall: 7.45 inches.
After quoting certain statistics, the paper concludes as follows:
As the saying goes: "It rained so much that no one remembers when it rained more." The "Union Catholique des Cultivateurs" and the chambers of commerce in the area keep protesting against the uncontrolled use of rainmaking machines, which are reportedly very active at this time. The national research council is even said to have selected the area for its experiments this year. Last year, a federal government B-25 aircraft is said to have passed the summer in the Abitibi, seeding the clouds.
On the other hand, some authorities vigorously deny having anything to do with the heavy rain-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
falls now occurring in western Quebec. However, learned articles have been written stating that no data are available on the effectiveness of rainmaking machines.
Those remarks seemed to imply: "Since we have no specific data, rainmaking machines are not doing any damage in the areas where they are used."
Meanwhile, our crops are getting a beating, our lakes and streams have swollen to levels unprecedented for this time of the year, and tourists are seeking fun and relaxation under different skies.
As early as 1958, the Val d'Or-Bourlamaque chamber of commerce had instructed the members of its tourist industry committee to inquire into the rumours to the effect that tests on a fairly large scale were being made in the area to induce rainfall by artificial means.
The committee which made the inquiry reported on January 14, 1959.
That report, in the form of a 28-page brief, contains very interesting information. I cannot list all the details here, but I might quote a few excerpts from the first two pages, which read as follows:
In compliance with the expressed wish of members of the Val d'Or-Bourlamaque chamber of commerce, we have looked carefully into the problem of artificial precipitation of rain and snow.
This report is a record of our research and interviews, and includes reprints of articles published in various newspapers and magazines that have shown interest, in recent years, in this matter which we feel is of the greatest importance for the stability and especially to the development of our tourist industry and our agriculture.
It is obvious, Mr. Chairman, that rainmaking equipment considerably increases normal rainfall, with consequent damage to our businesses, industries, settlers and farmers.
Indeed, as a result of our investigation, we have reached the conclusion that no control is being exercised over those rainmaking machines. Hotel-men and businessmen agree that there is a drop in the tourist trade. How can it be otherwise when we have had so little sunshine to offer tourists during the so-called "fair season," especially in the last two years.
The report then prints a whole series of articles from newspapers and scientific journals dealing with the possibilities of producing rain by artificial means. It also refers to certain experiments conducted in Canada and in the United States. I do not propose to read all those articles, but just the same I should like to read the conclusions of the report which is found on page 28 of the brief:
We must face the facts: scientists have developed a way to induce artificial rainfall. It seems that this discovery, which could be of great service to humanity, in periods of drought, is being used and applied by two large corporations whose apparent sole concern is to produce rainfall for the benefit

of a few customers, such as operators of logging companies and other such companies. Since there is no control over the operation of the machines, they are being used at the detriment of our local tourist industry and of our store keepers, contractors, engineers, air transport companies, prospectors, miners, workers, transport companies and farmers. They are also detrimental to the health of our local people, who are thus deprived of the precious benefits of sunshine, especially in a part of the country where summers are already relatively short.
We honestly believe that it is the duty of the Val d'Or-Bourlamaque chamber of commerce, at whose request we have undertaken the survey to call to the attention of people in larger centres, through their chambers of commerce and municipal bodies, to that abnormal situation, so that those same public bodies may undertake further research as a basis for representations calling for government action in controlling those rainmaking devices.
Mr. Chairman, so far this year we have an excessive amount of rainfall in northwestern Quebec, and people there are convinced that the experiments and tests carried out in the area in connection with artificial rain have something to do with it. The matter was first brought to their notice by articles published last May and June.
The first of those articles appeared in the Financial Post of April 2, 1960, and reads as follows:
(Text):
Many industries, governments and the military will be watching closely this summer as giant and repeated rainmaking efforts are made in Quebec's Rouyn-Noranda area. Private and government groups are backing the experiment, called precipitation physics project. Truly successful rainmaking could revolutionize farming, forest fire fighting.
(Translation):
The second article, which aroused the people's anger, appeared in the Imperial Oil Review for the month of June under the heading: "Water, Life's Pivot". Here is what it said:
Hatfield-
A scientist,
-had discovered "cloud seeding", a technique which is still being tested. At Val d'Or, Quebec, the national research council is conducting experiments on the seeding of clouds with silver iodide crystals. The final results are not yet known, but according to British and American tests, the technique increases rain precipitation by 10 to 15 per cent in hilly country.
In an article published in L'Echo Abitibien for July 7 last, and sponsored by the chamber of commerce of Val d'Or-Bourlamaque, we find the following paragraph:
We know that last year the same national research council sent a B-23 type plane to Val d'Or, in charge of sergeant Miller, to carry out cloud seeking and research work north of the city. We feel that we could very well do without it at this time.

And the article goes on to say:
How long will we, in the northwest, have to go on serving as guinea-pigs for experiments on the rainmaking machine, which surely has proven itself in our area over the last three years, despite statements to the contrary from some people who have a financial interest in trying to prove the opposite?
Then the article goes on to say:
We would suggest that letters be sent by the federation of chambers of commerce to the various departments concerned, asking for some control over those machines which could be operated for the welfare of the community, but which at present are subjected to no control and are operated for the benefit of a few large corporations.
I do not intend to deal much more extensively with this matter; however, I would like to say this. Following representations made by the chamber of commerce of Val d'Or-Bourlamaque, the Abitibi federation of chambers of commerce contacted the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and asked him to comment on this matter of artificial rain and on the experiments which are made in northwestern Quebec.
Following this correspondence between the federation and the Minister of Transport, the L'Echo Abitibien, of July 28 last, published a very interesting article from which I will quote a few excerpts. It is entitled:
Rain experiments in our region.
And the article begins as follows:
The population of western Quebec has just received not only a first implicit confirmation that this area is the site of experiments on weather modification, but has received an outright invitation to sacrifice itself for the advancement of science in this field.
The article then quotes parts of Mr. Hees' letter and adds the following comment:
According to the signer of the letter of July 22, the federation is said to have asked last spring for "discontinuance of experiments on precipitation", whereas, apparently, the local chambers of commerce have invariably asked for "control in the use of rainmaking equipment".
In any event, the minister says that when he inquired from his officials, they gave him the following explanation:
"As you know, the wide variation in atmospheric precipitations from month to month and from year to year, in a given locality, causes either a great lack of rainfall or excessive rainfall, as was the case this year in your area." We assume that the phrase "as was the case", used here, refers to "excessive rainfall" rather than to the words "lack of rainfall".
But let us go on. "The economic advantages", adds minister Hees, "which might result from an increase or decrease, through human intervention, of atmospheric precipitations at a given time and in a given place, would surely be considerable. Many experiments have been undertaken in order to discover the secret of the process of precipitation, and of the control or change of this precipitation".

After those general remarks, the minister admits that "even if this process is not adequately understood, many business firms have undertaken to increase precipitation and do away with hail in certain localities.
Because of inadequate knowledge of the physics of clouds and rain, and in view of the great difficulty of ascertaining the effects, if any, of those experiments, my department has been asked to assess the methods now in use to modify the weather."
"On account of the economic possibilities inherent in weather modification, added the minister, especially with regard to forest fire fighting, water power and agriculture, it has been decided that steps should be taken to increase scientific knowledge on the cloud and rain formation process, so that reasonably accurate information can be made available to all concerned."
Mr. Hees then deals with the experiments themselves. "Therefore, a scientific project has been launched for the detailed study of all aspects of cloud formations and precipitation.
An airplane equipped with special instruments studies the composition of clouds and carries out an extensive program of observation in the clouds and in thunderstorm areas. The rainfall accompanying such thunderstoms is recorded in detail in two test areas by means of ground instruments which show the curve of quantity and intensity of the rainfalls".
"Part of those tests, adds the letter, consists in making a comparison between clouds treated with chemicals and untreated clouds, in order to obtain a wider range of information on the rain formation process. In the present case, silver iodide crystals are used. This comparison is not in itself an attempt to increase or decrease rainfalls, but simply part of a general scientific investigation."
"As I know, concludes the minister, that members of your chamber of commerce are interested in man's ability to modify and control certain elements in nature, I believe that, now that they have more complete information, they will wait for the results of the test, instead of worrying about the damaging effects which might result from it."
"If you wish additional information, or if I have failed to describe certain aspects of the matter, please let me know", (signed by) Mr. Hees.
We suppose that the two chambers will find the minister rather reticent, even if he admits a good deal, and that they will, in fact, ask him some questions, more particularly about the necessary duration of those tests.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the most important point.
The people of northwestern Quebec through their chambers of commerce and other local organizations, are asking the relevant authorities to establish efficient control of the problem of artificial rainfall and of its rainmaking machines used in those tests. The request is a fair one, and I have good reasons to think that the government will give it all the attention it deserves. (Text):

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks on this vote for the

Supply-Trade and Commerce national research council. I think few Canadians would question the fundamental importance of research and increased research activity in this country. I have always felt that in a small country like Canada with our problems of exports imports, and the use of our vast store of natural resources, research on a per capita basis was even more important than in many other lands around the world. Like the hon. member for Hum-ber-St. George's, I would certainly hope that our committee on research which was set up this year, and which had a few meetings, could be set up again at an early date next session in order that we might continue our work of examining the national research council and other bodies involved in research in this country. There is very much that remains to be done in the way of increasing and sponsoring research by the government of Canada. Nevertheless I am proud, and I am sure other members of our party are proud, of the very important and creditable record of our government in the last three years in the field of government sponsored research.
Speaking from memory, if my recollection is correct our grants to the national research council, for instance, have about doubled during the period from 1956 or 1957 until 1960. This year we are talking of a sum in the neighbourhood of $33 million, which is a vast increase in such a short period of time and will certainly provide a stimulus to research in this country. A part of this increase is in a very important field, that is the area of scholarships and grants in aid to universities. Universities are a natural training ground for students, graduates, fellows, and teachers, and as a result of the mingling of the teaching staff with the research staff seem to me to be the best places where money can be used for the purpose of increasing research efforts in this country. The increased amount granted by the national research council for this, is certainly most stimulating.
I should like to mention briefly a most important document that was tabled the other day, and which I think could be referred to under this heading; that is the report of Dr. Farquharson's committee studying medical research grants and the aid that could be given to medical research by the government of Canada. I think it is fair to say, Mr. Chairman, that this document is the most important one of its kind in recent decades in this country. Its recommendations and its whole purpose are crucial to the medical profession and the people involved in medical research in Canada. As an aside, may I say I am hopeful that perhaps some day we will have the same sort of study,

and perhaps the same sort of decision eventually, in regard to an agricultural research council in Canada.
The recommendations contained in Dr. Farquharson's report are most interesting and I should like to refer to two or three of them. First there is the establishment of a separate medical research council under terms similar to those of the national research council. I am hopeful this recommendation will prevail with the government, and that the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance will recommend the establishment of this separate body in the near future.
There are several other recommendations that are worthy of note. For instance, there is the one that an interdepartmental medical research co-ordinating committee be set up to integrate the activities in medical research presently being carried on in the department of health and welfare, the Department of Veterans Affairs and the defence research board. There are recommendations involving finances to be used for the purpose of medical research, some of which relate to the budget of this proposed new council itself. There is mention of the sum of $4 million for this purpose, and then a reference to the large amounts of $25 million and $12 million respectively for new medical schools and for research facilities in hospitals. These amounts total approximately $40 million in all, and would provide a tremendous stimulus for medical research in our country. I was most interested in seeing the tables in Dr. Farquharson's report indicating government expenditures devoted to medical research in Canada, which in one column are expressed as percentages of the gross national product. These tables indicate that in the years since our government assumed office we have made some major increases in these expenditures. As a matter of fact they have been increased in the period 1956-57 to 1959-60 by almost 50 percent. Nevertheless, when one looks at tables I, II and III in this report one can see how far we are behind such countries as the United States in government expenditures for this purpose. The table indicates that we have a long way to go to catch up to the United States and other countries. This area is one to which the Prime Minister and the cabinet will have to give detailed consideration in the future. I believe this report marks a milestone in the study of research facilities and research funds for medicine in Canada.

The report of the special committee on research which sat during this session of parliament contains a recognition of the fact that the committee did not have an opportunity to do its work thoroughly. There is a reference to this in the report, as

I say, and I want to direct a specific question to the minister concerning it. The committee recommended that it be reconstituted early in the next session of parliament in order that it may continue its deliberations. This recommendation was made after the explanation concerning the difficulty of examining the subject matter in the limited time available. Is the minister in a position to give an undertaking now that the government will bring forward a motion to set up this committee at an early stage in the next session?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I feel very sure that will be done because of the importance of the study the committee will want to undertake. It did not have time to complete its survey this year. I am in agreement with the hon. member for Ottawa West that the committee should be re-established.

I have one other question with regard to the report to the minister by the special committee appointed to review government supported medical research. The report was tabled on August 6, and it is very interesting. I do not propose to discuss it today, but it contains some very specific recommendations for the setting up of a medical research council and refers, among other things, to the budget for that council. Has the government made any decision as yet on this matter? If so, what is that decision; and if it has not taken a decision when may we expect such a decision to be taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: In connection with the recommendations, not all of them have been adopted. The one concerning the setting up of the medical research council is approved and, so far as this year is concerned, it will be set up under the jurisdiction of the national research council. Subsequently, when we have had time to consider, it will become a separate entity, but for the moment it will come into being and will operate independently for all practical purposes, except that it is under the national research council for the presentation of estimates to the house.
It will carry on in the interim as an activity of the national research council alone, separate in form but under the legislation governing the national research council?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. It is quite separate, except that the national research council will be responsible for the administrative services required by the medical council.

Mr. Chairman, this vote deals with the atomic energy control board, and is perhaps the vote under which most appropriately can be discussed atomic energy and matters connected with the uranium industry which is the source of that energy.
This particular vote and the questions relating to it were considered by the special committee on research, but that consideration, Mr. Chairman, was very short and cursory. The committee had one meeting only on the question of atomic energy, during which it received a very interesting and valuable report from the president of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. After that report I think there was opportunity for five, 10 or at most 15 minutes' discussion, and that was that.
It is unfortunate, to say the least, that a matter of this importance received such limited and insufficient consideration by the committee. The president in his report explained the development of atomic policy in what I thought, although I was not at the committee meeting, was a very impressive way. He explained to the committee why the development of atomic energy was taking the form, so far as power is concerned, of the kind of nuclear reactor which is moderated by heavy water and fueled with natural uranium. There has been a great deal of argument as to this form of nuclear power development versus other forms. I am not qualified to express any opinion on that highly scientific matter, but we must all hope that the course along which we are moving in this connection will turn out to be the proper one.
Related to this question is the position of the uranium industry in this country as the source of atomic energy. It is clear, of course, to everyone who knows anything about this subject that our supplies of uranium are so great that whatever may be the developments in terms of the non-military use of atomic energy in Canada, we will be able to consume only a very small portion of this commodity. Therefore we have been and are still dependent on export markets for the maintenance of this industry. Above all we are dependent on the United States of America, which has taken in the past and is at present taking practically all of our production.
I was interested to read in the report of the president, at page 187 of the minutes of the meeting, that-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Canada has also been fortunate in its close collaboration with the United States since the war years.
That is, on atomic energy matters. I think we have been fortunate in our collaboration in the matters with which the president was dealing, but certainly we have not been so fortunate in the last year in our relationship to the United States as the market for our uranium production. As a result of the action taken by the United States government last August, I think it was, the industry and those communities which depend on the industry have received a very severe blow to their future development, and indeed to their very existence as communities.
The importance of this industry in our national economy is not appreciated by very many people because it is a new development. Most people are not aware that last year we exported more than $300 million worth of uranium, mostly to the United States. In the present year there will be a diminishing export, and in two or three years, unless something happens to restore the market for this uranium in the only place where it could be restored, the United States, our exports will have largely disappeared. It will be a very difficult period indeed which we will have to face until the world again needs our uranium as a source of energy. That is bound to come, but there is going to be a gap between that time and the end of our contract with the United States. The uranium communities, especially Elliot Lake which is the largest of them, have to prepare for some pretty lean days during that period.
While I understand the pressures in the United States from domestic producers, I think in refusing to take up the options which were in the original contract the United States has not asked in a way we might have expected from a neighbour and a friend which talks so much about continental collaboration in defence, which should mean industrial collaboration for defence as well as other forms of defence. In any event, as we know, the United States government did not take up any of the options last summer, and an arrangement was made between the two governments in Ottawa and in Washington for a stretch-out of existing contracts.
We have been told, Mr. Chairman, that the original contract, which was for five years, should have been negotiated on a longer term basis. We are told that we on this side, who were responsible at the time for the negotiation of this contract, should have realized then that there would be a decreasing market for uranium as the years went by, that therefore we should have


held out for a longer period, and that we should have anticipated this lessening demand and the difficulties ahead.
We on this side who were concerned with this matter at that time are told we should have taken this position in 1954 and in 1955, when the contract was negotiated. We were supposed to have known of all this at that time, although some years later when the situation was in fact changed because of the development of United States production, those on the other side who are now responsible for these matters were not themselves aware of the difficulties. The Minister of Transport made it clear in October, 1957 that in his view, and I quote, we could "now look forward to continued and extensive development in this field of the mining industry". By that he meant the uranium industry.
At that time the preoccupation in this house, when the matter came before the house and the committee, and in the minds of those concerned with this industry, was that we were tying up our production for too long a period of time rather than for too short a period of time. That caused a little difficulty at that time with the United Kingdom, which had to make special arrangements with us in order to get any share of the production which had been earmarked for the United States.
Therefore it is hard to appreciate why a situation which was not considered difficult in 1957 and 1958 should have been considered difficult in earlier years. Indeed, as late as July of last year spokesmen for the government, including the Minister of Trade and Commerce himself, said that we on this side were being too pessimistic when we said there was only one thing which could save the industry, and that was by intervening at the highest political level with the President of the United States to ensure, if it could be ensured, that these options would be taken up. That was not done and we have a stretchout instead, so the uranium communities are in difficulties.
When this matter came before the house- and I will resist the temptation to go through the record in Hansard-we were told that the government was doing something about this situation. We were told there was a factfinding committee. We were told the government was aware of the seriousness of the situation, and that there would be visits to Elliot Lake and other places. In answer to our request from this side regarding what was being done we were told to be patient. Finally in May we were told that another committee had been set up to look into the situation. As a matter of fact I think the first committee was set up in December, 1959 to

deal with this matter-the minister will correct me if I am wrong-so then we were told in May, 1960 that the remedy would be the setting up of another committee.
I am asking the minister if he can inform us what proposals have been made by this committee which even now might be of assistance. What, even now, can the government do to help these uranium communities to face the difficulties which have been created for them?
There are various things that could have been done. There are various things that have been considered very carefully by the province of Ontario as things that should be done. Indeed the province has taken action in some respects. If you really want to learn about the difficulties and what can be done, Mr. Chairman, you will get a great deal more information by reading the Hansard from Queen's Park than by reading the Hansard of Ottawa. That is where I get most of my information. That Hansard from page 1700 on quotes letters exchanged between Mr. Macaulay and the minister and gives a great deal of information as to what might be done to help the community of Elliot Lake.
I am not going into all the proposals made for such assistance. They have been made and rejected, so far as we know. The possibility of a nuclear research station for Elliot Lake was removed when the government decided to locate that station in Manitoba. The possibility of some financial inducements which would encourage new industry to move into this community seems to have been removed as far as I am able to ascertain. Certainly I know of one negotiation which has ended without anything being done. The possibility of a provost training school being established at Elliot Lake was removed by the Minister of National Defence the other night. The minister said it was going to Camp Shilo, and he thought the people of Elliot Lake would be in agreement with that decision. Well, he was wrong in that respect. I do know that the province of Ontario was willing to make available a school building for this purpose, but the department of defence considered the site not suitable, and so it goes. We do not know what steps if any are going to be taken in the federal field to assist these people who, without question, need help.
Of course there are other communities in Canada which have had misfortunes, and I would point out that sometimes they have received help. But this is a desperate situation for the uranium communities concerned. There is surely an obligation on both levels of government to do what can be done to meet the situation. That does not mean merely
Supply-Trade and Commerce setting up a committee. So perhaps we shall get a report from the minister as to what that committee has been able to do.
It is not hard to understand the action of the United States government in refusing to take up the options last summer especially in the light of reports, some of which I have before me, of the development of new uranium production in the United States since the action was taken in Washington. However that may be, the results are apparent, and I am asking the minister under this item if he can inform the committee even at this late date whether these committees which have been set up-the first of them last December, the fact-finding group some time in March and another committee in May- have been able to make any recommendations to the government which would meet this problem at least in part and, if so, whether the government is proposing to implement such recommendations.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am not sure whether the Leader of the Opposition and I are in the mood to get into too spirited a debate with regard to some of these problems. We discussed them at length in March and I have covered all the ground, all the arguments raised on the other side. It is just open to question whether there should be a repetition of those views on this occasion.
There appears to be some doubt as to what information was available at the time the uranium contracts were entered into. The Leader of the Opposition has indicated that there was some concern that Canada, by entering into those contracts, might be committing too much to the future if her contracts with the United States for uranium were extended beyond the five-year period. Of course it is getting in the background now as to what should or should not have been done several years ago, but I have in front of me an extract from an address by Mr. W. J. Bennett, who was president of Atomic Energy of Canada. The address was delivered to the Toronto board of trade in Toronto on January 24, 1955, five and a half years ago, and Mr. Bennett said this:
It is impossible to say at this time what the demand for uranium will be after March 31, 1962, the present expiry date of the guaranteed market. The military demand may continue at the present rate or may cease altogether. On the other hand, we may have a situation in which there is still government buying but on a reduced scale. Whatever happens, it can be safely predicted that there will be some requirement for uranium for use in atomic power programs in the early sixties. It is evident, however, that the demand for uranium in the early stages of a Canadian atomic power program will take up only a small part of our potential production. Consequently, if the military requirement ceases or is cut back substantially, Canadian producers may have to look to export markets

Supply-Trade and Commerce
and should expect to meet the same conditions which prevail in the case of other base metals which are not in short supply.
There were other examples of warnings given in 1955. In fact, in March I read the warning given in September of 1954 by the late Mr. R. J. Henry of Eldorado Mining and Refining Company indicating the discoveries of uranium in the United States, the mines operating there and the supply situation generally. I wonder at what the Leader of the Opposition expressed as Canadian concern at the time the contracts were negotiated that Canada might be signing away some of her uranium for too long a period if the contracts were for more than a five-year interval.
However, the situation has turned out just as Mr. Bennett thought it might. The military demand declined and therefore the demand for uranium declined. Then we got into a position where the options were not going to be taken up and a stretch-out program had to be arranged. Not sufficient attention has been paid to the value of that program.
What actually faced the uranium industry in Canada was the shutting down of practically all uranium mines in 1961 and 1962 unless a stretch-out program could be arranged. What faced us before that was the shutting down of some mines in 1959 and 1960, with the loss of the undelivered portions of their contracts. So the arrangement made with the United States was that a master contract would be written replacing the earlier contracts. That master contract would contain the total amount of uranium that was involved in the other contracts and the delivery of the uranium in the future-in 1960 and the following years-would be under that master contract so that not one pound of the uranium contracted for in the earlier contracts would be lost to Canada. Where mines were closed their contracts could be transferred to other mines, and the total production for Canada would not vary from what had been arranged originally in the contracts signed for the five-year period.
This has meant to the Canadian uranium industry $120 million that otherwise would have been lost and not available to Canada. In all the discussion that has been going on about the stretch-out program, the failure of the United States to take up the options, and the criticism of the Canadian government for not doing what it could have done in the opinion of some people, I have heard very little commendation for the action of the government in saving for Canada and the Canadian uranium industry $120 million that otherwise would have been lost. This factor is completely overlooked.

The second part of the stretch-out program has meant that uranium mines will be continued in operation for a longer period than otherwise would have been the case. In the three major areas where uranium is being produced the mines will be operating into the years 1963 and 1964, whereas not long ago the prospects were that they would all be closed down by 1961 and 1962. Very few people have bothered to commend the government for making this arrangement, yet it is important to the communities affected and it is important to the miners working in those mines. The stretch-out program has accomplished just that, and has provided for employment over a longer period of time.
Some people not in the mining business but interested in supplying the mining community with the services required have said that it would have been better if there had been no stretch-out program and the mines had closed down in 1961 or early 1962, because they would have operated full blast for five years and the commitments that certain people had made in the business communities could have been met in that five-year period based on the payroll of the communities working full out. That is one way of looking at it, but from the standpoint of the employment of miners I think it is better to have the stretch-out program that carries them forward for another three years.
In the western regions the Port Radium mine, which was the original mine, has been closed down because of lack of ore and will be out of production this year. Beaverlodge and Gunnar are staying open. The employment factor there, including Port Radium, is 1,300 men at the present time, in the latter half of 1960. During 1961, 1962, 1963 and running into 1964 employment will be maintained at about 1,150. I am speaking now of miners in the mines and personnel engaged right at the mines themselves.
In the Bancroft area two mines will remain in operation. The employment figure for 1960 is roughly 1,000. It will continue at that rate during 1961 and 1962, and I hope we will carry that forward into 1963. Certain adjustments have to be made which will make it possible for the Bancroft area to carry on well into 1963.
In the Elliot Lake area some mines have been closed and others are staying open. My information at the moment is that Quirke, Nordic, Panel, Milliken, Stanleigh, Denison and Stan Rock are in operation employing for the second part of 1960 just over 6,000 men. It is expected that in the first half of 1961 the employment figure will be close to 5,500 and then it will be reduced to 4,500 and run at that figure well into 1963.

These three mining communities have not immediately collapsed because of the change in the uranium program. Through the stretchout arrangements and the transfer of contracts, employment has been provided for almost 8,500 miners at the present moment, reducing by the end of 1962 to just over 6,000 and then in the latter part of 1963 to about 5,000. That is the over-all figure for the uranium industry.
By the end of 1963, however, we will have a much clearer picture as to the demand for uranium. It is my hope that there will not be a demand solely for military purposes, and it may be that a demand will be created in the field of peaceful uses of uranium. Perhaps by the time another three and a half years have elapsed other uses will have been found for uranium. Experiments are going on now which give some promise of success. Although the failure of the United States to take up the options has had an effect, although some mines have had to close down, and although the three communities mentioned have all been affected, nevertheless the situation is not as bleak as it has been painted. I am not so sure that we cannot do more. I believe that the stretch-out program came into being in order that those communities could be maintained. There is an adjustment period, of course, but that adjustment period is spread over three full years, 1960, 1961, 1962 and running into 1963.
The Leader of the Opposition has asked what has been done with regard to assisting the communities affected. An immense amount of time has been spent exploring the possibilities for assistance to the communities. Delegations have been met; individuals have been interviewed; a committee has been working at the job; and it has proved to be extraordinarily difficult to find immediately other means of employment for people in the three mining communities that I have mentioned. I have indicated, however, that employment is being sustained at rather a good figure; but to bring a new industry immediately into the area is not the easiest thing in the world to do. We have explored that to a very great extent. Some attractive leads appeared at various times but I cannot report that there has been success in some of those investigations.
We had nothing as a federal government in the way of an institution to put into any one of the three communities that I have mentioned. There was some discussion about the Department of National Defence placing one of its training schools in one of the communities, but the expense was very great and it seemed wiser to spend the money for defence in other ways than transferring a school to a community in which the army was not established.

Commercial firms have been interested in the community of Elliot Lake, but we have not been able to reach any particular settlement with regard to the transfer of certain commercial firms to that area. In the past I have commended the people of Elliot Lake on their enterprise in attempting themselves to attract industry to that area, but it is difficult to do that in mining areas, and we appreciate that fact. However, we are open to suggestions from any source with regard to what may be done to assist industry to establish in one of those three mining communities so that employment may be sustained.
In the course of the next three years it may be that mining for uranium in the mining communities may become more important from the standpoint of world demand, or it might be that other mines may be opened, producing other minerals. That is the situation. The people who are seriously affected by the dislocation in employment that has come about through no fault of their own have been a matter of great concern to the gvernment. They did not foresee this break in what appeared to be rather a good and continuing future, but the break has occurred and adjustment has to be made. My hope is that that adjustment can be eased a bit over the next three years. In some instances it will be eased; in others it has been rather abrupt and we regret, naturally, that those people should have suffered. But I can assure the Leader of the Opposition and the committee that a great deal of effort has been put into trying to find alternative schemes to assist the three mining communities affected. At the moment, as far as the federal authority is concerned, it is the stretch-out of the program which assures the miners another three years of employment which has seen the major part of our efforts along that line.

I do not want to prolong this discussion on what may conceivably be the last day of our session, but I want to deal briefly with one or two of the points made by the minister. He indicated that some of us did not understand or appreciate the advantages of the stretch-out. It should be clear, Mr. Chairman, that the stretch-out arrangement with the United States, while it prolongs the employment of the miners concerned, prolongs the employment of a smaller number of them because the stretch-out does not and cannot result, as I understand it, in the production of a single pound of uranium which was not provided for in the original contract. It is a difference, if you like, if I may put it in those terms, between sudden
7908	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Trade and Commerce death and a lingering death, I do not hesitate to say that the latter certainly is preferable. I have already said that the stretchout is something; it does provide, if you like, for a lingering death during the period of which you may be able to find the remedy that may mean you will not die at all; and I admit that is better than sudden death; but if no remedy is found during the longer period, then the result will be just the same. It will be the end of this industry in its present form.
One of the points the minister made-he repeated this many times-was that we should have known something about this. Mr. Bennett is quoted as indicating that there would be difficulties in the future, and we should have been aware of those difficulties. The fact remains that at the time this contract was signed the only observation made in this house about it was by the leader of the opposition of that day, and it was along the lines that I have indicated, wondering whether we were not tying up our production for too long a period, and when the matter came before the committee there was no suggestion made by anybody which would justify the kind of warning that we are given now in 1960. Indeed, as the London Economist pointed out a little while ago, dealing with the United Kingdom phase of this matter, and I quote from an editorial:
When the United Kingdom program was first drafted experts worried that the world production of natural uranium might not be sufficient to meet the United Kingdom needs.
This situation changed as soon as the United States began to explore and develop sources of uranium in its own country. It had every right to do this, but I suggest that the action should have been related to the commitments that the United States had made with Canada under its contract and its options. Once the United States began to ignore any such moral commitment and to find and to develop its own supplies of uranium in great quantities, then the whole situation changed and there was no possibility of getting out of this difficulty unless the matter was brought to the attention of the United States government in the terms which I have previously indicated. It was all right for them to find uranium, of course; but I suggest that in view of the relationship which existed between the two governments, having found that uranium, they were in honour bound not to develop it in a way which would prejudice the successful working out of the contract and its options. The United States did not do that, and once it became clear that the United States was not going to do that, then we were in trouble.

As I said in 1957, the only way we could get out of this trouble was on the highest political level. But the spokesmen for the government in 1957 did not think we were in trouble. I have already quoted the Minister of Transport. When we argued the case in the house along the lines I have stated it now, we were accused, as usual, of being prophets of gloom and doom. The doom has not descended on the industry but it is pretty gloomy and I certainly hope that something can be done to remove the gloom.
That brings me to the only other point I wish to make. What can be done? The minister has said that the government has worked hard. The committee has worked hard. I know that the hon. member for Essex South, who is head of the committee looking into this matter, has done very good and very hard work investigating the problem. I think anybody in the area from which I come is willing to acknowledge that, and I acknowledge it. I am grateful to him for the investigations he has made and for the way he has been willing at any time to receive anybody who had anything to say about this matter.
But the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, and I am quoting now from his statement on April 12, "The problem requires action on a broad front and that action is going forward." So far as we have heard this afternoon, in spite of the investigations that have been made and in spite of the work that has been done, it has not been possible for that action to go forward. I will only express the hope now that as a result of the work about which the minister has talked there will still be some possibility of action which will enable Elliot Lake and the other uranium communities to live over the very difficult period indeed that faces them to the time when they will face a far brighter future when uranium will be needed, we hope, for non-military purposes to an extent to which it is not required today.

Mr. Chairman, there was no money taken out of the exchange fund as the expression "taken out"

Supply-Finance
is ordinarily understood. There was absolutely nothing abnormal in any respect in any of the transactions carried on by the Bank of Canada as agent of the Minister of Finance in exchange transactions this year.
The function of the exchange fund is a very limited one, and it is unchanged. The method of operation is precisely what it was under our predecessors; there has been no variation or departure. This fund is not used with a view to directing the trend of the exchange rate. It is simply used day by day with a view to avoiding the sharp edges of the variations in exchange rates from time to time. There was no departure this spring at the time when there were rather active movements of the exchange rates from the basis of operation which has prevailed with respect to this fund for years. There have been some baseless slanders and accusations made in certain journals, one in particular in New York, that the Minister of Finance had taken advantage of an opportunity to reduce the exchange fund with a view to supporting the Canadian dollar and in this way to endeavour to counteract the rise in the value of the United States dollar and the decline in the value of the Canadian dollar in the month of May of this year. There were vague suggestions that this had been done deliberately with a view to reducing the amount of the exchange fund, and providing out of the proceeds Canadian dollars to supplement the cash available in the consolidated revenue fund. There is not one particle of truth in any of these accusations. The operations of the fund were completely normal in every respect.
Because there was such an active exchange market in the month of May, the transactions of the exchange fund were numerous, and because the trend of the Canadian dollar was downward in value the effect of the transactions was to bring about a reduction in exchange fund holdings of United States dollars. But this was only a temporary trend and the holdings of United States dollars in the exchange fund have risen since until at the present time they are approximately what they were at the end of April. I say to you, therefore, Mr. Chairman, there never was any truth in these vague slanders and accusations which emanated, in the first place, from New York. The operations were entirely normal in every respect, and the normal nature of the transactions is best reflected in the fact that by reason of the operations in the ordinary way, the way in which this fund has been operated for years, our holdings in the fund now are back approximately to what they were at the end of April.

Mr. Chairman, this is probably one of the most important votes that comes before us. At the same time it is probably one of the most complex to explain or understand. The question of financing is important and difficult on any level whether individual, family or government, as I am sure all hon. members will agree. Financing is always a difficult problem especially if you try to balance income with outgo. I do not pretend to be an expert on finance on a governmental

level even though it was my responsibility for some 12 years to be financial critic of the provincial budget in the legislature of British Columbia.
We could spend hours and days on this vote attempting to analyse the correctness or otherwise of government policy in relation to a balanced budget, a deficit budget, the question of conversion loans, the Bank of Canada, interest rates and many other aspects of finance. It is not my intention this afternoon to go into the complexities of these matters in any way whatsoever. I do not think they can be resolved at this time in this session.
The government has to accept responsibility for the financial policy; it has to face the criticism of the opposition. I still do not feel that I am in a position to discuss this matter, nor do I feel that anything of advantage would be gained by doing so at this time. All I want to do is to raise a matter which I think is of absolute paramount importance and ask the Minister of Finance whether he will comment on it. At the time of confederation, brilliant as they were, the fathers of confederation could not possibly foresee the development of the economy of Canada; they could not foresee the growth of Canada or the complex situations that would arise between the various levels of government in this country. Brilliant as they were, they could not foresee the responsibilities of the different levels of government in the establishment of what I might term the welfare state.
In recent years the complexities of government have reached a point where in our estimation, giving all honour to the fathers of confederation, the time has long passed when a good look should be taken at the responsibilities of all levels of government and their ability to accept them. Year after year we have seen the increasing complexity of the responsibilities of governments and their inability to meet them. We find that year after year the municipalities, the children of provincial governments, are screaming to high heaven and to the provincial governments for greater financial assistance. We hear the provincial governments year after year screaming to high heaven to the federal government for greater assistance to enable them to meet their financial responsibilities. To whom does the federal government scream for assistance? Of course, the federal government has only one answer. It is either no or a compromise with the provinces by utilizing its powers to make the taxpayers scream over an additional tax burden. In short, that is the situation. Surely under those circumstances we have now reached the time when an exhaustive analysis

and survey have to be made of the responsibilities of the various levels of government and their ability to meet them. As I said, Mr. Chairman, today's conditions could not have been envisaged at the time of confederation. We now have to face the realities of the situation. I say the time is long past when we can continue to ignore the changes that have taken place in the responsibilities of government and their ability to meet them. I am not recommending the appointment of a royal commission. I feel sometimes, and I have felt over the past few years, that we have reached the point of having royal commissionitis. We can go too far, but I do believe that the greatest contribution that can be made today by the federal government is to recognize the need for a review of the responsibilities of the three levels of government, their ability to pay, and work out something different from what we have at the present time under which the federal government assumes certain responsibilities in co-operation with the provinces. The provinces, according to their thinking, then pass some of the responsibilities onto the municipalities.
As I say, I do not believe in a royal commission or a three-day dominion-provincial conference, but in a longer study, whether it takes days, weeks or months, by experts of the departments of finance of the dominion, provinces and municipalities. They should call in all the experts they require to try to work out what I think is the greatest need today, namely a new look at the responsibilities of governments and their ability to meet them. I emphasize this because there are too many-and perhaps many of us are guilty of this-who think that they can make demands on government and get what they ask for for nothing. There is not one service that can be given by any level of government in Canada that can be received for nothing. There is nothing whatsoever that can be obtained for nothing from a government. It has to come eventually from the taxpayer's pocket, individually, collectively or co-operatively, and the ability to collect is based on the productivity of our nation through the work of our people or the natural resources of our country.
We know that the municipalities are up against a tough time at present. They can appeal to only one body, namely the provincial government. The provinces can appeal only to the federal government. The federal government has only one answer, namely no or new taxes. The sooner that we at all levels of government face up to that situation and the sooner the people learn that what they want they have to pay for the better 79951-0-500

From my experience in a provincial legislature and seven years in the House of Commons I do honestly believe that we have to sit down, giving all honour, as I said, to the fathers of confederation, and face up to the situation. At the same time let us recognize that now, almost 100 years later, having in mind economic development, technological advances, the new responsibilities of government and the interrelationship between the municipalities, the provinces and the federal government, a new look is required.
I am not going to go into all the complexities of the matters I mentioned when I first rose which could be discussed for hours and days, but I should like to ask the Minister of Finance whether he does not agree that the time has now arrived for this kind of study, review and new look at the responsibilities of governments in Canada and their ability to meet these responsibilities and to meet the new and ever increasing demands by the people of the country. That is an issue that we have ignored and have not faced up to in the past, and it is time that we did.

I am convinced that is the finest investment that could ever be made and that the extension of understanding within that group will perhaps make it the greatest instrument for peace.

Mr. Chairman, as it is my intention to limit myself to municipal financing because of the precarious condition that Canadian municipalities find themselves in at the present time, I should like to make an appeal to the minister to see if a more equitable distribution can be arrived at so that the municipalities can carry on the work they are meant to carry on. First of all, I should like to ask the minister this question. Is there an arrangement between the federal and provincial governments to share the expense of hospitalization or maintenance in

the case of immigrants or refugees coming into Canada? If I am not going to get a reply now, I will go on.
I am in total sympathy with the bringing in of refugees on compassionate grounds and also other immigrants but they should not be left to seek help from the provinces and municipalities; especially from the municipalities with their very limited powers of taxation. In other words, their welfare should remain the responsibility of the federal government.
As mayor of a municipality it has been my experience that after one year and one day immigrants who are unfortunate enough to become ill or indigent become the responsibility of the province and the municipality in which they reside. The cost of our social service division in Outremont has increased by approximately 300 per cent in the last three or four years.
The selection of these refugees and immigrants, whether on compassionate grounds or otherwise, is the responsibility of the federal government and the responsibility in the case of indigency or hospitalization should rest with the federal government until they are entitled to attain full citizenship. These neo-Canadians should not be left to the mercy of the municipalities which have not the means or the facilities to give them the help they need. They should remain the responsibility of the federal government for the first five years of their residence in Canada.
Canadian municipalities are experiencing unprecedented difficulties in their financing at the present time. The unwarranted high rate of interest on debenture loans is discouraging municipalities from undertaking capital expenditures and major works programs due to the high cost of providing the necessary moneys by bonds or debentures. Many pressing municipal works projects have had to be postponed and many essential ones that could not be delayed are reduced to the necessary minimum.
I come now to the question of tax exempt municipal bonds. Should the federal government exempt the interest on municipal bonds from income tax? This is the United States practice. I believe that as an alternative to such an exemption the government should establish an intergovernmental loan corporation or a national loan fund. The responsibility for the provision of appropriate funds at low interest rates should rest with the federal government. This corporation would be authorized to purchase the securities of municipal governments at a rate of interest which would reflect the cost of borrowing to the federal government plus a carrying charge, including in the computation of the

charge probable losses through defaults. The corporation should not be restricted to the financing of self-liquidating projects and should be authorized to buy the securities of any community whose economic capacity reflects the ability to pay for the loan over a fairly long period of time. This solution would provide assistance to municipalities, particularly the poorer ones, which are plagued by high interest costs.
If such a loan corporation or loan fund were established it would enable an attack on municipal problems on a much broader basis than that involved in the low cost borrowing made possible by tax exemption and would make unnecessary such a tax exemption even in a modified form. May I say that such a fund has been specifically requested by the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities and is also supported universally across the country by the municipal governments. I should like to read a short extract on capital borrowing from the national municipal program issued by the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities.
Because of the nature of their undertakings, municipal governments must necessarily finance most capital projects by loan financing. This requires that they have access to capital funds at a cost commensurate with the social purposes of municipal undertakings and within the reasonable capacity of a community to afford. If municipal governments are to keep pace with their growth requirements, renew obsolescent community facilities. and maintain their capital plant at a satisfactory standard of efficiency, they must be able to finance the cost of such improvements at the lowest rate possible.
Joint participation by the federal, provincial and municipal governments in the capital expenses of building waterworks, sewers, road building, paving, etc., would go a long way in placing the municipalities of Canada on a sounder financial basis and enable them to undertake many improvements that they could not otherwise go on with.
May I say here that the municipalities of Canada have a serious and justified complaint concerning throughways. They realize that local streets are a municipal responsibility but the principal cross-city thoroughfares of today's cities are no longer merely local streets. They are an integral part of a vast interconnected system of regional, provincial and national highways, and the cost of constructing these throughways should be apportioned and shared by all levels of government.
Within a short span of years the population of Canada has shifted considerably. In 1901 our rural population was 62.5 per cent of our total population and the urban population was 37.5 per cent. In 1951 the rural population had dropped from 62.5 per cent to 43.3 per

cent, while the urban population had increased from 37.5 per cent to 56.7 per cent of our total population. Forecasts have been made to the effect that in 1980 some 80 per cent of our total population will be living in urban areas. As a result of the shift in rural and urban populations the demand for increased municipal services and local improvements is growing at a rapid pace. Changing conditions give rise to newly expanded governmental activities. This, in turn, necessitates close governmental collaboration if the municipalities are to retain a reasonable standard of services for the local activities which cannot be financed from local taxes or other local revenue sources.
Municipal governments today need to have direct communication with the federal arm of government on a wide variety of matters. Urgent and involved questions are consistently arising which affect federal-municipal affairs, especially in matters of taxation and revenue. I should like to read a short extract from the booklet entitled "Canadian Public Administration" by Mr. George S. Mooney, executive director of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities:
Municipal governments are entitled to sufficient revenue to finance the activities required of them by custom or law. The revenues they need will be determined by the responsibilities they assume. Municipalities should not be expected to assume any additional or delegated responsibility beyond the just capacity of their taxpayers to afford, unless supplementary funds to cover the costs are forthcoming from the source originating the responsibility (i.e. federal or provincial governments). Expanded municipal services are possible only to the extent that expanding revenue resources become available.
A little farther on, the article states:
Because of the nature of their undertakings, municipal governments must necessarily finance most capital projects by loan financing. This requires that they have access to investment funds at a cost commensurate with the social purposes of municipal undertakings and within the reasonable capacity of a community to afford. If municipal governments are to keep pace with growth requirements, renew obsolescent community facilities, and maintain their capital plants at a satisfactory standard of efficiency, they must be able to finance the cost of such improvements at the lowest rate possible.
Under the present conditions of the money market the facilitating aid of the provincial and federal governments is necessary if municipal governments, particularly the smaller municipalities, are to be put in a position to continue a reasonable program of needed capital improvements.
The amount of the funded debt of most municipalities is already high and increasing rapidly. Many are near the dangerous limit of 20 per cent of the taxable property valuation. Municipalities in this percentage bracket find it extremely difficult to borrow money, no matter what their needs may be. The 79951-0-500i
Supply-Finance
heavy funded debt with which most municipalities are burdened, without having reached the 20 per cent mark, also prevents them from undertaking the borrowing of the money necessary for the carrying on of projected works programs and capital expenditures. Sewers, water works, roadways and necessary improvements are in many cases at a standstill due to lack of funds. The high rates of interest prevailing is another factor that prevents municipalities from borrowing to carry on the improvement programs they badly need.
The municipal taxpayers cannot bear heavier municipal taxes than they are now paying. Hundreds of municipalities have practically reached the bankruptcy stage. The impossibility of municipalities, because of the reasons mentioned previously, to carry on necessary works programs is contributing greatly to the unemployment situation existing today. A 5f per cent interest rate, which municipalities are for the most part called upon to pay, is the cause of great unrest, uneasiness and worry to municipal administrations whose problems are growing more and more complex every day. The range and scope of municipal administration is increasing steadily.
There has been a phenomenal increase in the demands of citizens for additional and better services and municipal corporations, because they are at a lower level than the senior government bodies, exercise but a small influence in the elaborate control structure in comparison to the federal and provincial governments. I should like to read from "Canadian Public Administration", which contains an article entitled "Democracy and Local Government" by Mr. Hugh Whalen, associate professor of political science, University of New Brunswick. I quote:
The local taxing authorities are caught between two millstones. The upper one consists of the top limit of the burden of taxation which it is feasible to impose upon the taxpayers, and still leave them intact financially and leave their representatives intact politically. The position of the nether stone is progressively raised as the amount of the total municipal expenditure ... increases. Thus, the play between the two is continuously reduced and the capacity of the taxing authority, the council, to provide the services demanded by the public is narrowed. Caught as they are in this squeeze, councils are driven to continuous appeals to the provinces for financial assistance or additional sources of revenue. But there is likely to be a reluctance to make available to municipalities any really productive sources of revenue, for most provinces are themselves sufficiently desperate for additional funds that they would hesitate to release them to a subsidiary level of government.
Municipal administrations are finding it more and more difficult to balance their budgets. Their powers of imposing taxation

Supply-Finance
are greatly limited and unless the higher governments, such as the federal and provincial governments, grant them relief from many of the responsibilities they now bear the situation is bound to become intolerable. In order to help municipalities to undertake any needed works programs in which it would be necessary to borrow to meet the capital cost, senior governments should lend money to municipalities at a lower rate of interest than that at which they themselves borrow.
I should like to quote some figures which I have taken from the Canadian tax foundation, November 1959 issue, on local finance. The total taxation in Canada was raised in the following proportions in the year 1933 as compared with 1958:

Federal	39.4	278 million	61.8	4,652 millionProvincial	18.9	133 million	21.3	1,605 millionMunicipal	41.7	294 million	16.9	1,275 million
It will be seen that federal and municipal governments collected practically the same percentage of the total taxation in 1933, federal 39.4 per cent and municipal 41.7 per cent. By 1958 the federal share had increased from 39.4 per cent or $278 million to 61.8 per cent or $4,652 million of the total taxation and the municipal share had decreased from 41.7 per cent to 16.9 per cent. Is it any wonder that the municipalities have now almost reached the bankruptcy stage? Is it any wonder that the municipalities are clamouring for a more equitable distribution and a fairer share of the total taxation in Canada?
Unlike the flexible, varied and multiple sources of revenue available to federal and provincial governments, the revenue sources available to municipal governments are both rigid and limited. As a consequence muncipal governments have been operating within a financial strait-jacket wherein there is room neither to adequately meet the backlog of unmet accumulated need for local public works, nor to meet in any degree commensurate with the need the pressing requirements which accelerated urban growth and expansion are forcing upon them.
Most of our municipalities were conceived and designed in an earlier period. To meet present needs it is necessary to widen and provide more costly streets, provide off-street parking, expressways, underpasses and overpasses and other costly traffic and transit improvements. Most water and sewer systems, sewage and refuse disposal facilities, street lighting, civic buildings and other services are obsolete and need to be renewed. Slum clearance on a large scale is now a necessity

and provision of minimum standard housing for low income families must receive immediate attention.
There has been a relatively high and sustained volume of municipal capital borrowing during recent year. Most of this borrowing has gone to meet the costs of deferred public works which piled up during the depression and war years. In 1939 the total outstanding debt of all municipalities in Canada was $1,225,400,000 and in 1958 had reached $3,384,700,000. Muncipalities meet with considerable difficulty when they have to borrow. Small municipalities find it extremely difficult to market their debentures and some have found no market at all for their bonds.
The fixed burden which municipalities have had to assume has increased greatly in recent years. Many municipal taxpayers are experiencing hardship in meeting their local tax obligations and could not stand an increase no matter how small it might be. Yet the city fathers are faced with a difficult situation. They must either raise the local tax rates or cease immediately all work on municipal projects. The municipal governments are genuinely concerned about their financial situation-their available resources are stretched to the limit.
Certain it is that the revenues presently available are inadequate. The needs of most municipalities have reached a critical stage. Many municipalities have reached the point where further capital expenditures cannot be financed. The borrowing of money must be made easier for the municipalities. They cannot continue to undertake the construction and building of necessary local and capital improvements unless money is made available at a lesser rate than the present one. The municipalities can no longer bear the heavy burden under which they are operating.
With respect to the federal government, many phases of federal legislation impinge upon or directly affect municipal governments. There are frequent occasions when the particular problems of municipalities involve federal action and require federal-municipal collaboration. On such matters as health, welfare, indigency and hospitalization the position of municipal governments should be made clear with respect to federal and provincial legislation. Problems which limit and hamper the effectiveness of local government administration and thereby weaken the whole structure of our democratic system of government should receive special consideration from our senior governments.
It is my hope that municipal government in Canada can be lifted to the really important place it deserves, both in fact and in public

estimation. I believe that a joint conference of the governments at all levels should be held and the municipalities should be invited to discuss the present problems confronting them. The Prime Minister and his colleague, the Minister of Finance, might take advantage of the meeting with the premiers of the provinces of Canada in October to prepare the way for a future conference with representatives of the municipalities of Canada.
Before closing I should like to refer to an article in the Financial Post of August 6, 1960. That article says that there has been a 40.7 per cent drop in government, provincial, municipal and corporation public bond financing in Canada for July, 1960. The total financing in July, 1959 was $150,757,500 and this total dropped in July, 1960 to $89,324,225. The municipal financing last month amounted to $12,298,225; 20 issues from Quebec and the maritimes, 11 issues from Ontario and six issues in western Canada. This, compared with the amount of $24.6 in July, 1959, represents a drop of practically 50 per cent.
